deep_why: The core challenge is predicting which users will respond to ads and promotions given very little history for new campaigns. The method works because training a single model on all objectives (streams, clicks, follows) forces the model to learn shared patterns across diverse user behaviors and contexts. When the model learns what makes content appealing generally, it can apply that understanding to new advertising goals even without examples of those specific goals. The shared knowledge of user preferences and content characteristics serves as a bridge: instead of starting from scratch for a new campaign, the model transfers what it learned about persuasion and engagement from thousands of existing interactions. This reduces the cost-per-stream because the model can immediately make reasonable decisions for cold-start users rather than wasting impressions on random exploration.

Dynamical networks are systems where the structure itself changes based on activity—edges form or fade, weights shift—making them inherently uncertain. Quantifying uncertainty means establishing bounds on how wrong predictions could be given incomplete information about the network's current state and parameters. The guarantee comes from rigorous probability accounting: if you measure the range of plausible network structures and their dynamics, you can compute which predictions remain valid across all possibilities and which break under some but not others. This matters because networks are fragile—small changes in topology can flip a system from stable synchronization to cascading failure—so knowing the range of outcomes prevents false confidence. For epidemiology or power grids, this framework transforms vague worry into actionable risk: you know how much room for surprise exists and can design safeguards accordingly.

Real graphs are huge and storing them wastes memory, so the goal is creating a much smaller graph that still teaches the model the same patterns. The method works by representing many nodes as discrete codes (like hashing nodes to a codebook), then checking which nodes are structurally similar by looking at their neighborhoods. If two nodes reach the same neighbors in similar patterns, they can share the same code without breaking the model's understanding. The low-rank approximation captures the essential structural pathways—skipping noise—and the discrete codes make storage efficient. This works because graph patterns are hierarchical: most information flows through a small set of core structural motifs, so you can compress aggressively while preserving what the model needs to learn.

The attacker must inject fake nodes into a graph while fooling both the model and any defenses, which is hard because small discrete choices (add this edge or not) don't allow smooth tuning. The method sidesteps this by using reinforcement learning to treat the problem as sequential decisions rather than one-shot choices, making the discrete problem learnable. The softened embedding smooths the discrete choices temporarily during learning, then hardens them back to valid graph changes for actual attack. This works because learning via incremental trial-and-error beats local optimization on discrete choices—the model explores many possibilities and learns what patterns of connections fool both the original model and defenses. The defense-aware policy means the learner adapts as defenses respond, rather than assuming a fixed target.

Knowledge bases contain patterns like 'author → paper → author' for finding collaborators, but nobody writes these patterns down explicitly. The goal is discovering which retrieval paths work best from data about what queries succeed. The approach uses a bi-level loop: one level explores which patterns might help, and another level learns how to score items using those patterns. This works because successful retrievals implicitly reveal useful patterns—if query X finds good results by following path A, that path must be relevant to understanding what query X meant. By coupling pattern discovery to retrieval success, you avoid guessing; the data itself shows you which patterns matter. This beats manual rule writing because the learned patterns adapt to what the system actually needs rather than what designers imagine.

Graph-based recommendation learns from user-item interactions, but random augmentation (adding fake edges or removing real ones) disrupts this signal. The method applies diffusion to gently perturb the graph: instead of random changes, it denoises a noisy version of the graph structure, preserving the low-rank structure that matters while erasing incidental noise. This works because diffusion naturally separates signal from noise—the core interaction patterns are robust to small perturbations while accidental correlations fade away. For long-tail items (those with few interactions), the approach uses conditional diffusion, letting global graph structure guide the denoising so that rare items inherit the statistical strength of frequent ones. This works because rare items actually do share causal patterns with frequent items; using global signal to fill gaps leverages that hidden similarity.

Real recommendation systems receive images, text, creator info, and user history—many different sources—but need to produce a single unified ID representing what to recommend. The challenge is aligning these sources so a user's visual preferences align with what text says about the item. The method trains a network to learn which parts of each input correspond to the same semantic meaning across modalities. This works because the world's structure is the same whether you describe it in words or pictures; if text says 'action movie' and images show explosions, they point to the same thing. By learning to recognize that correspondence and fusing the aligned signals into one ID, the system gets a richer, more reliable ranking signal than any single view alone.

Fake news detectors look for specific cues in articles and comments that suggest misinformation. The attack goal is appending human-like comments that fool the detector. The method uses interpretability analysis to find which tokens (words or concepts) the detector weighs most heavily, then prompts a language model to generate comments using those influential tokens. This works because detectors rely on surface patterns, and if you use the exact language patterns the detector associates with fake news or real news, you can mislead it. The underlying principle is that detectors are only as robust as the least common feature they trust—exploit that weak point and the entire judgment flips. Pairing interpretability with generation ensures the attack is both targeted and credible rather than random noise.

News believability depends on subtle cues: causal language, qualifications, acknowledging counterevidence. The attack makes small, targeted edits—removing qualifiers, shifting causality, hiding caveats—that shift readers' trust in the story. This works because human judgment of credibility relies on these linguistic markers as heuristics; people subconsciously trust language that acknowledges complexity and doubt words that oversimplify. By making minimal, context-aware changes, the attack preserves the surface story so casual readers miss the manipulation, while the edits systematically weaken the linguistic signals of careful reporting. This exploits the gap between what a headline literally says and the tone of authority it conveys.

Code generation requires multiple skills in sequence: understanding the problem, choosing an algorithm, describing the solution, then writing code. Current benchmarks only measure the final result, missing where reasoning breaks. The approach breaks evaluation into phases and measures each separately. This works because skills are interdependent—a weak choice of algorithm dooms the code even if syntax is perfect, and weak problem understanding ruins algorithm selection at the root. By measuring each phase independently, you see where models actually fail, not just whether the final output runs. This reveals that progress in one phase directly enables progress in the next, showing that the path to improvement is building the earlier skills first.

When judging whether an article is relevant multiple times, prior judgments unconsciously bias later ones—you expect consistency even when items genuinely differ. Psychological research shows certain personality traits reduce this bias. The method simulates these personality profiles in the language model through prompting. This works because personality profiles encode stable reasoning patterns: someone high in openness considers diverse perspectives and is less rigid in applying first impressions; someone low in neuroticism stays calm and doesn't spiral into anxiety-driven confirmation bias. By instilling these reasoning patterns through the prompt, the model carries them through the judgment sequence, naturally reducing the pressure to match earlier answers.

Auditing YouTube's recommendations requires mimicking real users at scale while staying reproducible, but real users are chaotic. The framework uses language models to simulate coherent user personas with consistent interests and behaviors. This works because coherent personas reveal systematic patterns in how algorithms personalize: instead of each user being random noise, you see how the algorithm responds to consistent signals. Personas are reproducible—run them again and get the same context—while still being realistic enough to trigger genuine algorithmic behavior. Decoupling contexts from personas means you can isolate what matters: is the algorithm reacting to stated preferences, viewing history, or both? This design turns a black-box system into an auditable one.

Portfolio optimization is constrained by the user's comfort with risk: someone might accept a volatile strategy if it offers higher returns, or might refuse it. The goal is generating diverse portfolios that respect the user's risk appetite. Traditional approaches either optimize for one solution (rigid) or forecast time series, then optimize (complex and misaligned). The method treats the portfolio itself as something to sample from a distribution, not as a point to find. This works because diffusion naturally generates diverse samples while respecting constraints: during denoising, you specify the risk level as a conditioning signal that guides the denoising toward portfolios matching that risk. This is simpler than forecasting futures because you directly learn the distribution of good portfolios from data rather than trying to predict what markets will do.

Attacking a recommender system means injecting fake users that shift recommendations. Existing attacks use simple heuristics or brute-force exploration. The method uses language models to behave like realistic users, generating ratings and reviews that feel authentic. This works because recommender systems learn from behavioral signals: if a fake user rates and reviews items coherently, the system treats it as real signal rather than obvious manipulation. Language models trained on human review patterns can generate text that mimics authentic voice and reasoning, bypassing the casual scrutiny that catches obviously fake content. By combining strategic fake-user profiles with realistic behavior generation, the attack becomes stealthier while having more impact than methods that either oversimplify or require insider knowledge.

Language models can rank items and explain why, but their explanations often miss the real reasons they rank something high—the reasoning sounds plausible but disconnected from what the model actually learned about user preferences. The method forces the model to explicitly reason through recommendations step by step using chain-of-thought prompting, then measures how uncertain that reasoning is. When reasoning is shaky, the method downweights it in favor of direct ranking signals. This works because explicit reasoning surfaces hidden assumptions: writing out steps forces the model to check its logic and catch flaws. Quantifying uncertainty identifies when the reasoning is post-hoc storytelling versus actual causal thinking. By adaptively blending explicit reasoning with learned signals, the system gets explanations that are both interpretable and grounded in what the model actually knows.
